---
title: "Benchmark: what the package adds on top of Arrow when reading"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = TRUE)
results <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path("..", "..", "bench", "results", paste0(name, ".parquet"))
  tibble::as_tibble(arrow::read_parquet(path))
}
read <- results("read")
counters <- results("read-counters")
knitr::read_chunk(file.path("..", "..", "bench", "read.R"))
has_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

This article reads stored results; it does not run the benchmark. The script
is `bench/read.R`; its code is shown below as it was run.

## Question

`store_read()` resolves the dataset in the catalog, picks a location, builds
an Arrow dataset from the catalog's file list, prunes partitions on the
catalog's partition values, lets Arrow scan, and then restores the R types
Arrow does not restore by itself and turns WKB geometry into `sf`. How much
time does all this add to Arrow reading the same files, for full reads,
column subsets, key filters and partition filters?

## Setup

```{r}
env <- read[1, grep("^env_", names(read))]
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  item = sub("^env_", "", names(env)),
  value = vapply(env, function(v) as.character(v[[1]]), character(1)),
  row.names = NULL
))
```

`r format(read$rows[[1]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` rows of
`rcs_sim_table()` (15 columns, among them `integer64`, difftime, a list
column, factors and two time zones) written once as one file and once
partitioned by year, and as many `rcs_sim_polygons()` rows in one file, all
in a local store on SSD. Methods:

- `store`: `store_read()`;
- `arrow_read_parquet`: `arrow::read_parquet()` on each file of the catalog's
  file list, bound together; a filter is applied in R after reading, except
  that the partition filter reads only the file of that year when the
  dataset is partitioned (the path is taken from the catalog);
- `arrow_open_dataset`: `arrow::open_dataset()` on the file list, with
  `dplyr::filter()` and `dplyr::select()` pushed down, then `collect()`;
- `arrow_sf` (polygons only): `arrow_read_parquet` plus turning WKB into
  `sf`, the decoding `store_read()` also does.

The Arrow methods return Arrow's own types: `integer` for small
`integer64` values, seconds for difftime, `arrow_list` for list columns, WKB
for geometry. Each method is timed with `bench_run()` (five repetitions after
one untimed run, warm file cache, median reported).

## Results

```{r}
ratio_to <- function(method) {
  vapply(seq_len(nrow(read)), function(i) {
    ref <- read$median_s[read$case == read$case[[i]] & read$method == method]
    if (length(ref) == 1) read$median_s[[i]] / ref else NA_real_
  }, numeric(1))
}
read$x_open_dataset <- ratio_to("arrow_open_dataset")
read$x_read_parquet <- ratio_to("arrow_read_parquet")
shown <- read[c("dataset", "operation", "method", "rows_returned", "median_s", "min_s", "x_open_dataset", "x_read_parquet")]
shown[5:8] <- lapply(shown[5:8], signif, 3)
knitr::kable(shown, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

`x_open_dataset` and `x_read_parquet` are the median time divided by that of
the Arrow method on the same operation.

```{r, eval = has_ggplot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Dot chart of median read time in seconds, one panel per dataset, one row per operation, with points for store_read, arrow read_parquet, arrow open_dataset and, for polygons, arrow plus sf decoding. The package's points lie to the right of open_dataset's on most operations."}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(read, aes(x = median_s, y = operation, colour = method)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~dataset, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Median seconds (log scale)", y = NULL, colour = "Method") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Work counters of `store_read()` (files opened and row groups in them):

```{r}
shown <- counters[counters$counter %in% c("file_open", "row_groups_total", "rows_returned"), ]
shown <- stats::aggregate(n ~ case + counter, data = shown, FUN = sum)
wide <- stats::reshape(shown, idvar = "case", timevar = "counter", direction = "wide")
names(wide) <- sub("^n\\.", "", names(wide))
knitr::kable(wide, row.names = FALSE, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

## Verdict

```{r, include = FALSE}
r <- function(dataset, operation, column = "x_open_dataset") {
  signif(read[[column]][read$dataset == dataset & read$operation == operation & read$method == "store"], 2)
}
```

- Tables: a full read through `store_read()` takes
  `r r("sales/one", "full")` times as long as `open_dataset()` on the same
  file (`r r("sales/by_year", "full")` times for the partitioned copy). A
  profile of the same read on 1e5 rows puts 70% of its time in restoring the
  list column: `restore_list()` rebuilds it element by element through
  `[[` on Arrow's `arrow_list` (a vctrs class, so every element access is
  an S3 dispatch). Dropping the class first and stripping attributes only
  where there are any gave the identical column five times faster. Arrow
  alone returns the column as `arrow_list`, `integer64` as `integer` and
  difftime in seconds.
- A column subset without such columns costs about what Arrow costs
  (`r r("sales/one", "columns")` times), and so does the key filter
  (`r r("sales/one", "key_filter")` times; Arrow skips row groups by their
  statistics because the file is sorted by the key).
- The partition filter on the partitioned copy opens only the file of that
  year (the catalog's partition values), yet takes
  `r r("sales/by_year", "partition_filter")` times as long as
  `open_dataset()` and `r r("sales/by_year", "partition_filter", "x_read_parquet")`
  times as long as `read_parquet()` on that one file: the
  `r format(read$rows_returned[read$dataset == "sales/by_year" & read$operation == "partition_filter"][[1]], big.mark = ",")`
  rows returned carry the list column, whose restoring takes half of the
  time in a profile; the rest is opening the dataset over all files before
  pruning.
- Polygons: with geometry, `store_read()` takes
  `r r("shapes/polygons", "full")` times as long as `open_dataset()` and
  `r signif(read$median_s[read$dataset == "shapes/polygons" & read$operation == "full" & read$method == "store"] / read$median_s[read$dataset == "shapes/polygons" & read$operation == "full" & read$method == "arrow_sf"], 2)`
  times as long as Arrow plus the same WKB decoding with
  `sf::st_as_sfc()`. The decoding is nearly the whole cost: `sf` computes
  each geometry's bounding box in R. Decoding the same WKB with
  `wk::wk_handle(wk::new_wk_wkb(x), wk::sfc_writer())` (wk is already
  imported) gave an equal `sfc`, with the same bounding box, about 16 times
  faster on 1e5 polygons.
- Without geometry, a polygon read costs what Arrow costs.

## Limits

- One machine and its SSD, warm file cache; two other agents ran tests and
  rendered documents while this benchmark ran.
- The Arrow methods do not return the same R types as `store_read()`; they
  show the floor that Arrow sets, not an equivalent result.
- Reads from a cloud bucket are in `benchmark-cloud.Rmd`; spatial queries in
  `benchmark-spatial.Rmd`.
